title: Arlo and Tansy's Perfect Paint Mix
markdown:
The morning sun, a brilliant golden disc, peeked over the tallest trees and painted the dew-kissed leaves in amber and rose. Arlo the bridge builder stretched, grin spreading like a second sunrise. Today was the day. His new sturdy bridge — weeks of planks and bolts, his best work yet — was ready for its first splash of colour.

“Hoo-hoo!” Tansy the squirrel landed with a soft thump on his shoulder, bushy tail a fluffy question mark. “Colors, Arlo! What colors for your bestest bridge ever?”

Arlo steadied her with a sturdy hand. “Pots and pots, Tansy. Brilliant blues like a summer sky. Sunny yellows like buttercups. Daring reds that shout.” He flourished toward a wooden table crowded with paint. “This bridge deserves to be the most spectacular sight in the forest.”

Tansy jigged on his shoulder, claws tickling his ear. “Spectacular!” She hopped down and nudged a pot of deep sapphire blue. “This one first. The deepest part of the pond.”

Arlo dipped a broad bristly brush. The paint came up thick, almost like sticky paste. He splashed it onto a wide plank. “A bit clumpy. Not quite flowing.”

Tansy, eager and perhaps a little too helpful, grabbed sunny yellow and tipped extra water from a nearby jug. She wanted splashy brightness. The yellow did not splash. It fled the brush, a watery streak, sad rivulets down the wood.

“Oh dear.” Arlo looked from lumpy blue to watery yellow. They tried mixing. The blue turned a muddy dull green-brown, miserable as a rainy Tuesday. The yellow paled it further, a faded ghost. Gloopy. Drippy. Disappointing. The paints refused to look bold. They simply looked sad.

“This is not spectacular!” Tansy’s whiskers drooped. The wood looked sadder than ever under the hopeful sun.

Auntie Noor bustled past, announced by the scent of freshly baked berry muffins — sweet ripe berries and warm dough. “Good morning, my dears. What a frightful mess you’ve got yourselves into.”

Arlo pointed a dejected finger. “We’re trying to paint the bridge, but the colours won’t mix. Gloopy and clumpy, or thin and drippy.”

Noor set down her tray, golden-brown tops dusted with sugar. “It’s like baking. You can’t throw things in a bowl and expect a perfect cake.” She picked up a plump muffin, berries peeking. “For these I need exactly two cups of flour, one cup of sugar, and just a little milk — not too much, or they turn to mush.”

Arlo looked from muffin to pots. “Ingredients in the right amounts?”

Tansy had been watching Noor pour a tiny bit of water into flour, then a splash of milk. The batter swirled, smooth as a creamy cloud. She remembered creek mud: a little water made it sticky, perfect for dams; too much and it ran away like a tiny muddy river.

“The water!” Her tail flicked. “Too much makes it run. Too little makes it clumpy.”

Arlo caught it. “Runny paint — like your mud. The right amount of water. Not too much, not too little. The ratio!”

They took fresh pots and did not hurry, though the morning was still bright with wanting. Arlo measured two scoops of bright blue. Then a small splash of water, no more than a teaspoon. They stirred. Thick, wonderfully smooth. It glided onto the brush with a satisfying whisper. Two scoops of sunny yellow. The same small splash. A golden hue that gleamed even in shade. They dared a dab of red with a bit of the blue, and instead of dull green-brown they got a brilliant rich purple, like a royal cloak.

“It’s working!” Tansy somersaulted on the grass. “Not gloopy. Not drippy. Perfect!”

They painted without rushing, even though the morning still wanted to be a race. Arlo’s brush laid down a vibrant blue that sang against the wood, plank by measured plank. Tansy’s paws smeared sunny yellow like pure joy, stopping to check the mix whenever it threatened to remember the jug. The purple sat between them, a deep gem along the rail. A jay landed, considered the spectacle, and left a remark that was probably rude. The colours lay smooth, inviting, spectacular at last, and the dew had burned off before they noticed.

Auntie Noor handed Arlo a blue plank to admire. She did not make a speech. The muffins did some of the talking: two cups, one cup, a little milk. The bridge did the rest.

Arlo’s chest puffed, just a little. “A ratio. Not too much, not too little. The right amount of everything.”

Tansy bounced on a freshly painted plank, then thought better of wet paws and bounced on the grass instead. “What other secrets can ratios unlock?”

Arlo licked a smear of yellow from his thumb, which tasted of nothing like buttercups, and grinned. Tomorrow they could ask the world another careful question. Today the bridge dried in the sun, two scoops to a teaspoon, as exact and as happy as a muffin that had decided not to be mush.
characters: Arlo (a bridge builder), Tansy (a squirrel), Noor (an aunt)
author: StoryGen Community
